extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students who write police/crime stories
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on selecting, shaping, and presenting police news and crime stories so they are fair, accurate, constructive, and appropriately dramatic while minimizing harmful effects on readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of story
rubrics_metrics.description: Since police news ranges from slight misdemeanors to the most serious of crimes such as murder and suicide, it offers widely different material for news stories. Because of the general interest in the material with which stories of crime deal, the purely informative story is sufficient in itself to insure reading. The strong personal element in stories of wrong-doing gives occasion for effective human interest presentation in the informative story. Amusing aspects of minor offenses, and even of burglary, hold-ups, or fraud, often furnish inspiration for humorous treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the form (informative, human-interest, humorous) based on the seriousness and social interest of the crime; examples and cross-references are given (e.g., 'Burglary,' 'Murder of Business Man', 'Charged with Intoxication', 'Hold-up').

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — consider effect on reader
rubrics_metrics.description: In no other kind of news should the effect of the story on the reader receive more careful consideration than in news of crime. The evil effects of news stories of criminal acts on many readers have already been pointed out. That these destructive influences can be offset to a considerable extent by constructive handling of news has also been shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always weigh how the story may influence readers (destructive vs constructive effects) and shape reporting to minimize harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterrence — show the crime is wrong and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that the crime story may have a deterrent effect, the crime must be shown to be wrong, even though the wrong-doer deserves some sympathy. The results of wrong-doing, not only in the form of legal punishment imposed but in the remorse and the pangs of guilty conscience that the wrong-doer suffers, as well as in the disgrace that he brings to others through his criminal acts, when emphasized in news stories tend to deter others from risking the dangers of such penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize legal punishment, remorse, shame, and other consequences to deter imitation; balance sympathy with clear presentation of wrongness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize underlying causes and responsibility when constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive presentation of crime news may also include emphasis on underlying causes and responsibility, especially when these can be traced to bad conditions in the community or in society as a whole, since such emphasis leads readers to consider the necessity for changing the conditions that are directly or indirectly responsible for the criminal acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use causal/contextual reporting to prompt public discussion of remedies; if the criminal is a victim of circumstances, it may be legitimate to create sympathetic understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sentimental treatment or heroization of wrong-doer
rubrics_metrics.description: A danger in writing stories of crime lies in creating sympathy for the undeserving wrong-doer by a sentimental treatment of him and his act. By making more or less of a hero of him, news stories may lead undiscriminating readers to regard him and his crime as not unworthy of emulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not romanticize criminals or their acts; avoid portrayals that could glamorize criminal behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice truth and accuracy for picturesqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is also a temptation in writing crime stories to sacrifice truth and accuracy of detail in order to secure greater picturesqueness or stronger dramatic situations, but such treatment is an indefensible deviation from the fundamental duty of presenting the news fairly and accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain factual accuracy above dramatic effect; never invent or exaggerate details for drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence should come from selection and presentation, not editorializing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever influence a story of crime may have on the reader should be the result of the reporter’s selection and presentation of the actual facts. Moralizing or 'editorializing' concerning the facts is not only unnecessary but undesirable in news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let facts and their arrangement convey the message; avoid overt moralizing or opinionated commentary in the news story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment — use dramatic narrative and vivid description if true
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic narrative and vivid description, when true to the facts of the news, are both legitimate and commendable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ narrative and description to make stories engaging only when they adhere strictly to the facts; use confessions, interviews, witness accounts, and clues to create effective narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep consistently to one point of view in presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to keep consistently to one point of view in arranging and presenting the details, particularly in constructive stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shifting perspectives that could confuse readers or undermine the story's constructive aim; organize details coherently around a single viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available material: confessions, interviews, witnesses, and clues
rubrics_metrics.description: Available material for making the narration and the description effective includes confessions, interviews with witnesses and persons involved, and clues to the identity of the perpetrator or to the solution of any mysterious phases of the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather and incorporate primary material (confessions, interviews, clues) to substantiate the narrative and maintain factual grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — give accused and accusers a hearing; proper labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness requires that persons accused of wrong-doing as well as their accusers be given a hearing in news stories. It must also be remembered that a person accused of crime is not a criminal unless he has been convicted; until he has been found guilty, he is described as an 'alleged' criminal, or is said to be 'charged' with the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek comment from both sides; use cautious language ('alleged', 'charged') until conviction; maintain balanced reporting of allegations and defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents — number of lives destroyed or endangered
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) number of lives destroyed or endangered
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scale of human cost as a primary factual element in crime reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents — names of victims
rubrics_metrics.description: (2) names of victims
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide victim identification when appropriate and consistent with privacy, legal, and ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents — names of persons charged with the crime
rubrics_metrics.description: (8) names of persons charged with the crime
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report identities of the accused when available, using appropriate qualifiers (e.g., 'alleged') and being mindful of libel and ongoing investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents — arrests of suspects and detention of witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: (4) arrests of suspects and detention of witnesses
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report arrest and custody developments accurately, noting official sources and statuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents — clues to the identity of the perpetrators when unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: (5) clues to the identity of the perpetrators when these are not known
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include investigative leads and clues, clearly labeled as such, without conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents — causes, motives, and responsibility (known or conjectured)
rubrics_metrics.description: (6) causes, motives, and responsibility, known or conjectured
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report motives and causes carefully, distinguishing between established facts and speculation; contextualize responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents — amount and character of loss
rubrics_metrics.description: (7) amount and character of loss
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify and describe material and non-material losses resulting from the crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents — methods employed in commission of the crime
rubrics_metrics.description: (8) methods employed in commission of the crime
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe modus operandi where relevant to public understanding and investigation, avoiding instructional detail that could enable copycats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents — measures to prevent similar crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: (9) measures to prevent similar crimes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report on prevention efforts, policy responses, or practical steps to reduce recurrence; include expert or official recommendations where available.
